page.text:
Integration in the complex plane constitutes the geometric and topological heart of
complex analysis. In single-variable real analysis, integration $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$
takes place along a fixed line segment whose path is unique up to orientation.
In $\mathbb{C}$, by contrast, integration occurs along directed continuous curves
(contours), offering uncountably many paths between any two endpoints.

The fundamental link between complex integration and the Cauchy--Riemann equations
is revealed by decomposing the differential $f(z)\,dz$ into its real and imaginary parts:
$$ \int_\gamma f(z)\,dz = \int_\gamma (u + iv)(dx + i\,dy) = \int_\gamma (u\,dx - v\,dy) + i \int_\gamma (v\,dx + u\,dy). $$
If $\gamma$ is a closed curve bounding a simply connected region $D$, Green's theorem in
the plane transforms these line integrals into double integrals:
$$ \oint_\gamma (u\,dx - v\,dy) = \iint_D \left(-\frac{\partial v}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right) dx\,dy, \quad \oint_\gamma (v\,dx + u\,dy) = \iint_D \left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\right) dx\,dy. $$
Both double integrals vanish identically by virtue of the Cauchy--Riemann equations
$u_x = v_y$ and $u_y = -v_x$.

Thus, Cauchy's Integral Theorem expresses the conservative nature of holomorphic differential
forms: contour integrals along closed loops vanish, path integrals depend only on the homotopy
class of the curve, and values in the interior of a domain are completely governed by boundary
data through Cauchy's Integral Formula.
